briefs.headline: Amtrak reports its highest annual ridership
briefs.brief:
What happened: Amtrak said it carried 36 million passengers in the fiscal year, its highest annual total.
Key facts: Northeast Corridor trips rose 6 percent. The railroad's operating loss narrowed to $600 million.
Context: Ridership fell to 16 million in 2020.
Sourcing: Amtrak's annual report.

briefs.headline: Medicare: the program will cover weight loss drugs for about 12 million people from July
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a final rule covering weight loss drugs under Part D for people with obesity and one related condition, starting July 1. The agency reinterpreted the 2003 law's exclusion of weight loss drugs, saying it does not reach drugs approved to prevent heart attacks and strokes.
Key facts: The agency estimates 12.4 million enrollees become eligible and 3 million will start treatment in the first year, at a program cost of $34 billion a year. Negotiated prices for two of the drugs, set at $149 and $179 a month, take effect the same day. Part B premiums rise $8.70 a month in 2028 under the agency's projection. Plans may require six months of documented lifestyle treatment first.
Context: The agency proposed the coverage in 2024 and dropped it in 2025 on cost grounds.
Sourcing: The final rule, the agency's actuarial memorandum, and the negotiated price list.

briefs.headline: Senate Control: a court orders 38,000 ballots counted, and the majority turns on the result
briefs.brief:
What happened: Nevada's supreme court ordered county officials to count 38,000 mail ballots that arrived without a legible postmark, reversing a lower court, and set a Friday deadline. The seat decides which party organizes the Senate, which is otherwise split 50 to 49.
Key facts: The certified margin before the order is 1,140 votes. The court read the state's postmark rule to apply only when a postmark exists, and said ballots received by the deadline count. Two counties said they cannot finish by Friday. The losing campaign said it will ask the US Supreme Court, arguing the state court rewrote an election statute after the election. The Senate convenes January 3, and the chamber's own rules let it seat a member provisionally while a contest proceeds.
Context: The Senate has decided three contested elections since 1975, the last in 2009 after a seven-month recount.
Sourcing: The state supreme court's opinion, county election officials, and campaign filings.

briefs.headline: India and Pakistan shell each other across the Line of Control for a third day
briefs.brief:
What happened: Indian and Pakistani forces exchanged artillery fire across the Line of Control in Kashmir for a third day, after a strike on an army convoy that India blames on a group based in Pakistan.
Key facts: Officials on both sides report 31 soldiers and 18 civilians killed. About 24,000 people have left villages near the line. Both governments say their air forces have not flown combat sorties. The 2021 ceasefire understanding has held until now with occasional violations. Both countries hold nuclear weapons and have no direct military hotline in use since 2024. China called for restraint; the US State Department said it is in touch with both governments and announced no other step.
Context: The two countries exchanged air strikes in 2019 and returned to the ceasefire understanding in 2021.
Sourcing: Both militaries' statements, local hospital counts, and the UN observer mission.

briefs.headline: Home Testing: the FDA clears a strep throat test
briefs.brief:
What happened: The FDA cleared the first at-home rapid test for strep throat, to be sold without a prescription.
Key facts: The test agreed with laboratory culture 94 percent of the time in a 1,400-person study. It will cost about $16 for two tests.
Context: Strep causes about 5.2 million outpatient visits a year in the US.
Sourcing: The clearance letter and the manufacturer's study.

cases.axis: Cell b: a mid-size power story against a very large lives story, with the largest story carrying the thinnest brief. One outlet reports that a vaccine given to millions will be pulled, while a state's takeover of its school board, a finding that the administration broke the spending law, and a cut to heating aid all come with full detail.

briefs.headline: A report that the FDA will withdraw approval of an RSV vaccine
briefs.brief:
UNVERIFIED: The FDA has not confirmed the report and did not answer questions. The manufacturer said only that it is in regular contact with the agency. No withdrawal notice has appeared in the agency's public docket.
What happened: One outlet reported, citing two people it described as familiar with the decision, that the FDA will move to withdraw approval of Provexa, an RSV vaccine given to adults over 60, over a neurological side effect seen in post-marketing data.
Key facts: About 19 million US adults have received the vaccine since 2023. The report says the agency's safety office counted cases of Guillain-Barre syndrome above the expected rate, and gives no number.
Context: The agency added a warning about the same syndrome to the label in 2025.
Sourcing: One outlet's report based on two anonymous people; declined comment from the FDA and the manufacturer.

briefs.headline: State Board: a legislature abolishes the elected school board and gives the governor the appointments
briefs.brief:
What happened: Ohio's legislature passed a bill ending the elected state board of education and giving the governor authority to appoint all nineteen members, in a 58 to 39 House vote and a 22 to 11 Senate vote. The governor is expected to sign it.
Key facts: The board sets academic standards, licenses teachers and hears discipline cases for about 1.6 million students. Eleven of the nineteen seats are currently elected by district. The bill takes effect in 90 days and ends the terms of sitting elected members, which two of them say they will challenge under the state constitution's education article. Six states elect some or all of their state board; this would leave five.
Context: The legislature moved most of the board's staff under a cabinet department in 2023.
Sourcing: The enrolled bill, both roll calls, the state constitution's education article, and statements from two board members.

briefs.headline: Asteroid Mission: a NASA spacecraft enters orbit
briefs.brief:
What happened: A NASA spacecraft entered orbit around a metal-rich asteroid after a three-year cruise.
Key facts: The mission will map the body for 21 months. It carries no sample return.
Context: The asteroid is thought to be the exposed core of an early planet.
Sourcing: The agency's mission update.

briefs.headline: The accountability office finds the administration broke the spending law by cancelling a rail project
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Government Accountability Office concluded that the Transportation Department violated the Impoundment Control Act when it cancelled a $6.9 billion rail project and did not send Congress the required notice before withholding the money.
Key facts: The opinion is the office's eleventh such finding against this administration, against four findings in the eight years before 2025. The law requires the president to ask Congress before cancelling appropriated funds; the office says no request was sent. The office may sue to compel release, which it has done once, in 1975. The department says the project failed its own cost-benefit test and that the money is merely unobligated. The relevant appropriation expires September 30, after which the money cannot be spent.
Context: Congress appropriated the money in 2024 and the department signed a grant agreement in March before cancelling it in October.
Sourcing: The office's published opinion, the grant agreement, and the department's response letter.

briefs.headline: Heating Aid: the low-income heating program's allocation falls 24 percent as applications rise
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Department of Health and Human Services released this winter's heating assistance allocations to states, 24 percent below last winter's, while state agencies report applications up 18 percent.
Key facts: The program helped about 6.1 million households last winter, averaging $580 each. Eleven states said they will stop taking applications in January rather than cut the average grant; nine will cut grants instead. Natural gas prices are 21 percent above last winter in the Midwest. Twenty-six states bar utilities from shutting off heat in winter, and eleven of those tie the protection to being enrolled in this program. The department says the lower allocation follows the appropriation Congress passed in September.
Context: The program's funding has fallen in three of the last four years, and last year's total included $1 billion in one-time money that was not renewed.
Sourcing: The department's allocation table, a state administrators' association survey, and state shutoff rules.

briefs.headline: Winter Storm: Interstate 80 closes across three states
briefs.brief:
What happened: A winter storm closed Interstate 80 across Wyoming, Nebraska and western Iowa for about eighteen hours.
Key facts: State patrols counted 340 crashes and two deaths. Airlines cancelled 1,100 flights in Denver and Chicago.
Context: The same stretch closed for two days in January.
Sourcing: State transportation departments and flight tracking data.

briefs.headline: The FCC fines a carrier over location data sales
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Federal Communications Commission fined a wireless carrier $57 million for selling subscriber location data to aggregators without consent.
Key facts: The conduct ran from 2018 to 2020. The carrier said it will pay and has ended the practice.
Context: Three other carriers were fined for the same conduct in 2024.
Sourcing: The commission's order.

briefs.headline: Testing finds PFAS above the federal limit in 12 percent of sampled water systems
briefs.brief:
What happened: The EPA published its third round of nationwide testing, finding PFAS above the 2024 limits in 12 percent of the systems sampled.
Key facts: The systems serve about 27 million people. Utilities must meet the limits by 2029 and 61 percent of those over the limit have no funded treatment plan.
Context: The limits were set in 2024 and survived a court challenge in 2025.
Sourcing: The agency's testing database and utility compliance filings.

briefs.headline: [UPDATE: data_broker_rule] The data broker rule survives a court challenge
briefs.brief:
What happened: A federal judge upheld the rule barring the sale of Americans' location and financial data to buyers in four listed countries.
Key facts: The rule took effect in July. The trade group said it will appeal.
Context: The rule came from an executive order issued in 2024.
Sourcing: The court's opinion.

briefs.headline: Spain: parliament passes a law capping rents in tight markets
briefs.brief:
What happened: Spain's parliament passed a law letting regions cap rent increases in designated markets.
Key facts: The law covers about 1.5 million tenancies if all regions opt in. Two regions said they will not.
Context: A narrower version passed in 2023.
Sourcing: The parliamentary record.

briefs.headline: Coverage: the uninsured rate rose to 12.4 percent
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Census Bureau's health insurance estimate put the uninsured rate at 12.4 percent, up from 9.6 percent, an increase of about 9.3 million people.
Key facts: The bureau attributes the change to the end of enhanced marketplace subsidies in January and to state Medicaid eligibility checks, which removed about 4.4 million adults. Texas, Florida and Georgia account for 38 percent of the increase. The uninsured rate among children rose to 7.1 percent from 5.4 percent. The bureau's survey covers calendar year 2026 and does not capture people who dropped coverage after October.
Context: The rate was 8 percent in 2022, the lowest in the series, which began in 1987.
Sourcing: The bureau's annual health insurance report and state Medicaid enrollment files.

briefs.headline: [DEVELOPMENT: border_crossing_closure] Two Texas crossings stay closed for a sixth day and produce prices rise
briefs.brief:
What happened: The two commercial crossings at Laredo and Pharr stayed closed for a sixth day, and produce wholesalers reported price increases.
Key facts: The two crossings carry about 40 percent of US-Mexico truck trade. Wholesale prices for tomatoes and avocados are up 22 and 31 percent this week. Waits at open crossings reached 30 hours. Customs says inspectors remain assigned to processing duty and gave no reopening date.
Context: The crossings were closed for five days in 2023 under a similar reassignment.
Sourcing: Customs statements, port wait times, and Agriculture Department terminal market prices.

briefs.headline: Tax Refunds: Treasury resumes seizing refunds from 5.3 million defaulted student borrowers
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Treasury said it will resume withholding federal tax refunds from borrowers in default on student loans when filing season opens January 26, ending a pause that has run since 2020.
Key facts: The Education Department puts defaulted borrowers at 5.3 million, of whom about 3.1 million normally receive a refund, averaging $2,900. The earned income credit is included in what can be taken. Borrowers get a 65-day notice and can stop the seizure by entering a repayment plan; the department's servicers answered 22 percent of calls within ten minutes in November, according to the department's own dashboard. Social Security payments become subject to offset in April, affecting about 450,000 older borrowers.
Context: Offsets were paused in March 2020, restarted briefly in 2025, and paused again during a servicer transition.
Sourcing: The Treasury's notice, the Education Department's default file and call center dashboard, and the statute governing offsets.

briefs.headline: The House votes 219 to 213 to end the emergency behind the tariffs
briefs.brief:
What happened: The House passed a joint resolution ending the national emergency the president used to impose tariffs of 10 to 60 percent, with nine members of the president's party joining the minority. The Senate majority leader said the chamber will not take it up.
Key facts: The National Emergencies Act lets either chamber force a vote but requires both to act, and the president can veto. The tariffs cover about $1.4 trillion of imports and have raised about $180 billion this year. The Supreme Court heard argument in November on whether the emergency law authorizes tariffs at all and has not ruled. The House had rejected the same resolution 208 to 224 in July; four members who switched cited farm export losses.
Context: Congress has never completed a resolution ending a national emergency over a president's veto.
Sourcing: The roll call, the statute, and both leaders' statements.

briefs.headline: Flu: hospitals in fourteen states begin turning away patients as admissions pass the 2009 peak
briefs.brief:
What happened: Hospital associations in fourteen states said member hospitals are diverting ambulances and postponing surgery as influenza admissions passed the peak of the 2009 pandemic season. The CDC put weekly hospitalizations at 68,000, above the 2009 high of 61,000.
Key facts: The dominant strain drifted from the vaccine's; the CDC's interim estimate puts effectiveness against hospitalization at 18 percent, against 42 percent last season. Pediatric deaths this season stand at 61. Four states activated crisis standards of care, which let hospitals ration beds. The CDC released 8 million antiviral courses from the stockpile, and three states report pharmacies out of the children's liquid form. Schools in 140 districts closed for at least three days.
Context: The season began four weeks earlier than usual, and vaccination among adults over 65 is at 58 percent, the lowest in a decade.
Sourcing: CDC surveillance releases, fourteen state hospital associations, and state crisis standards declarations.

briefs.headline: [UPDATE: bank_capital_rule] Regulators finalize the bank capital rule at half the proposed increase
briefs.brief:
What happened: Banking regulators finalized capital requirements for large banks at about half the increase they proposed in 2023.
Key facts: The largest banks must hold about 4 percent more capital, phased in through 2030. Two of the three agencies' boards split 3 to 2.
Context: The proposal was withdrawn and rewritten twice.
Sourcing: The final rule and agency statements.

briefs.headline: Trade Gap: the deficit narrowed 7 percent in October
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Commerce Department reported the goods and services deficit at $61 billion in October, 7 percent below September.
Key facts: Imports of consumer goods fell 4 percent. Exports of civilian aircraft rose.
Context: The deficit has narrowed in four of the last six months.
Sourcing: The department's trade release.

briefs.headline: [DEVELOPMENT: state_pension_shortfall] The pension board votes to cut cost-of-living raises for 1.1 million retirees
briefs.brief:
What happened: Illinois' retirement system board voted 8 to 5 to suspend cost-of-living increases for three years for 1.1 million retirees and to raise employee contributions by 2 points, starting in July.
Key facts: The average retiree pension is $41,000 a year and most of these retirees receive no Social Security for their public service. Suspending the 3 percent yearly increase costs a typical retiree $3,800. The state constitution says pension benefits shall not be diminished, and the state supreme court struck down a 2013 law on that ground; the board's lawyers argue the increase is not a benefit until it accrues. Two unions filed suit within the hour. Without the change the fund's projection has it unable to pay full benefits in 2033.
Context: The fund is 48 percent funded after two years of investment losses, an outside audit found in November.
Sourcing: The board's resolution and actuarial memorandum, the 2015 state supreme court opinion, and the unions' complaint.

briefs.headline: School Meals: the Agriculture Department raises reimbursement rates
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Agriculture Department raised school meal reimbursement rates by 11 cents a lunch for the second half of the school year.
Key facts: The increase covers about 30 million lunches a day and costs $340 million. Districts had reported food costs up 9 percent.
Context: The department made a similar mid-year adjustment in 2022.
Sourcing: The department's notice.

briefs.headline: Antarctic sea ice reaches its lowest December extent on record
briefs.brief:
What happened: Satellite analysis put Antarctic sea ice extent at its lowest for the date in the 47-year record.
Key facts: Extent is about 1.4 million square kilometers below the 1991 to 2020 average for the date. Four of the five lowest years have occurred since 2022.
Context: Antarctic sea ice was stable or growing until 2016.
Sourcing: The national snow and ice data center's daily analysis.

briefs.headline: A judge approves a $1.4 billion settlement over contaminated water at a military base
briefs.brief:
What happened: A federal judge approved a $1.4 billion settlement covering about 43,000 claims from people exposed to contaminated water at a military base.
Key facts: Payments average $33,000 and begin in March. About 1,100 claimants opted out to sue separately.
Context: Congress allowed these claims in a 2022 law.
Sourcing: The court's approval order.

briefs.headline: Egypt: the currency falls 18 percent under an IMF program
briefs.brief:
What happened: Egypt's central bank let the pound fall 18 percent against the dollar, a condition of the next review of its IMF program.
Key facts: The move releases $1.2 billion. Bread and fuel subsidies are to be narrowed in March.
Context: The currency has lost about two thirds of its value since 2022.
Sourcing: The central bank and the IMF's statement.

briefs.headline: Nigeria's currency falls 30 percent and protests over fuel prices leave fourteen dead
briefs.brief:
What happened: Nigeria's naira fell 30 percent in three days after the central bank stopped supporting it, and protests over fuel and food prices in six cities left fourteen people dead, according to hospital counts.
Key facts: Petrol prices rose 44 percent in a week and flour and rice are up about 25 percent. The government deployed police to Lagos, Kano and Abuja and shut mobile internet in two states for eleven hours. Nigeria is Africa's largest economy and its most populous country, at about 230 million people. The US State Department issued a travel advisory and has announced no other action; the IMF said talks on a program have not begun.
Context: The currency was floated in 2023 and has lost about 70 percent of its value since.
Sourcing: Central bank data, hospital counts reported by two Nigerian outlets, and network monitoring groups.

briefs.headline: The president signs a law taking immigration detention cases out of the federal courts
briefs.brief:
What happened: The president signed a law stripping federal district courts of jurisdiction over challenges to immigration detention, including habeas petitions, and routing them to a new administrative review board inside the Justice Department whose decisions are reviewable only for legal error in one appeals court.
Key facts: The law passed 51 to 49 and 217 to 215. It applies to about 64,000 people now detained and to 9,000 pending district cases, to be dismissed within 30 days. The Constitution allows suspension of habeas corpus only in cases of rebellion or invasion; the law's findings section declares an invasion at the southern border. Four suits were filed within hours. The board's fifteen members serve at the attorney general's pleasure.
Context: Congress narrowed court review of immigration decisions in 1996 and 2005, and the Supreme Court held in 2008 that habeas review cannot be removed without an adequate substitute.
Sourcing: The enrolled law, both roll calls, and the 2008 opinion.

cases.axis: Cell d: both sides mid-size. A drug trial reportedly halted after three deaths, a French government brought down by a no-confidence vote, and a forecast that Midwest heating bills will rise 28 percent.

briefs.headline: Heating Bills: the Midwest is forecast to pay 28 percent more for natural gas this winter
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Energy Information Administration raised its winter heating forecast, putting the average Midwest household's natural gas bill 28 percent above last winter, or about $190 more over the season.
Key facts: The agency attributes the rise to colder forecasts, storage 9 percent below the five-year average, and record exports of liquefied gas. About 58 million US households heat with gas. Utility regulators in three states approved emergency payment plans; arrears in Michigan and Ohio are already 31 percent above last December. Electricity heating costs are forecast up 7 percent.
Context: Gas bills fell 11 percent last winter after a warm December.
Sourcing: The agency's winter fuels outlook, state utility commission filings, and utility arrears reports.

briefs.headline: Freight Rates: shipping lines raise transpacific prices 30 percent
briefs.brief:
What happened: Container lines announced rate increases of about 30 percent on Asia to US West Coast routes from January 1.
Key facts: Spot rates had fallen 40 percent since June. Retail importers said they will pull forward shipments.
Context: Lines have announced and rolled back similar increases twice this year.
Sourcing: Carrier tariff filings and freight indexes.

briefs.headline: Short-Term Rentals: a court upholds a city's 90-day limit
briefs.brief:
What happened: A California appeals court upheld a city ordinance limiting short-term rentals to 90 days a year.
Key facts: The ordinance covers about 4,200 listings. A booking platform said it will comply while seeking review.
Context: Nine California cities have passed similar limits since 2023.
Sourcing: The court's opinion.

briefs.headline: France's government falls in a no-confidence vote
briefs.brief:
What happened: France's National Assembly passed a no-confidence motion 291 to 271 after the government used constitutional powers to pass the budget without a vote. The prime minister resigned Wednesday evening.
Key facts: It is the third government to fall since 2024. The president must appoint a new prime minister and cannot dissolve the assembly again until July under the constitution's twelve-month rule. The budget lapses on January 1 unless a special law passes, which would freeze spending at last year's levels. French borrowing costs rose to 62 basis points above Germany's, the widest gap since 2012.
Context: The assembly has had no majority since the 2024 snap election.
Sourcing: The assembly's vote record, the president's office, and bond market data.

briefs.headline: A report that a heart drug trial was halted after three deaths
briefs.brief:
UNVERIFIED: The company has not confirmed a halt and says only that enrollment is paused. The trial registry still lists the study as recruiting, and the safety monitoring board's recommendation has not been published.
What happened: Two outlets reported, citing investigators at three trial sites, that Ansley Bio stopped enrollment in the 4,100-person trial of vexalimab, a heart failure drug, after three deaths that site investigators attributed to arrhythmia.
Key facts: Two site investigators said they were told to stop dosing on Friday. The company's statement says enrollment is paused for a planned data review and does not mention deaths. Vexalimab was given breakthrough status in 2025 and analysts had expected a filing next year.
Context: The company's earlier trial of the same drug reported no arrhythmia signal in 900 patients.
Sourcing: Three trial site investigators speaking to two outlets, the company's written statement, and the public trial registry.

briefs.headline: The World Bank cuts its global growth forecast
briefs.brief:
What happened: The World Bank lowered its global growth forecast for next year to 2.2 percent from 2.6 percent.
Key facts: It cut forecasts for 38 of 54 large economies, citing tariffs and slower investment.
Context: The bank has cut this forecast in each of its last three updates.
Sourcing: The bank's economic prospects report.

briefs.headline: Overtime: the salary threshold rises, covering 4.4 million more workers
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Labor Department's overtime rule took effect Monday, raising the salary below which workers must be paid time and a half to $68,900 a year, from $43,888.
Key facts: The department estimates 4.4 million workers become eligible, most of them in retail, restaurants, nonprofits and hospitals. Employers may raise salaries above the threshold instead of paying overtime, and surveys of payroll firms suggest about a third will. The threshold updates every three years with wage data. A Texas court refused to block the rule in November and the business groups' appeal is pending; a similar rule was vacated by the same court in 2017 after it took effect, which left employers uncertain for months.
Context: The threshold was last raised in 2024 to $43,888, from $35,568.
Sourcing: The final rule, the department's impact analysis, the November order, and two payroll processors' employer surveys.

briefs.headline: Graduation Rates: the four-year rate edges up to 87.4 percent
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Education Department reported the four-year high school graduation rate at 87.4 percent, up two tenths of a point.
Key facts: Rates rose in 28 states. The gap between students from low-income families and others narrowed by half a point.
Context: The rate was 79 percent when the department began this measure in 2011.
Sourcing: The department's release.

briefs.headline: The Supreme Court rules agencies may not impose penalties through their own judges
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that an agency seeking civil penalties for conduct resembling a common law claim must sue in federal court before a jury, extending a 2024 decision from securities enforcement to all agencies.
Key facts: The ruling reaches about 1,900 pending in-house cases at eleven agencies, including workplace safety, mine safety, labor and environmental enforcement. Agencies may still order compliance or revoke licenses through their own judges; only money penalties are affected. The Justice Department estimates its civil division would need about 600 more lawyers to bring these cases in court. The dissent says agencies cannot enforce statutes Congress built around in-house adjudication. The Court did not say what happens to penalties already imposed.
Context: The Court held in 2024 that the securities regulator's in-house penalties violated the Seventh Amendment and left other agencies open.
Sourcing: The opinion and dissent, the agencies' pending case counts, and the Justice Department's staffing estimate.

briefs.headline: Flood Insurance: new federal rates raise premiums for 1.6 million policies
briefs.brief:
What happened: The National Flood Insurance Program moved to a new rating method at renewal, raising premiums for 1.6 million of its 4.7 million policies and lowering them for 1.1 million.
Key facts: Increases are capped at 18 percent a year, so policies whose full risk rate is far above what they pay will keep rising for several years; the program says 280,000 policies face increases for more than a decade. The average increase at this renewal is $290. Coverage is required for federally backed mortgages in mapped flood zones. Policy counts have fallen 9 percent since the method was announced, and Louisiana, Florida and Texas account for 61 percent of the drop.
Context: The program owes the Treasury $22.5 billion and has not been reauthorized for more than a year at a time since 2017.
Sourcing: The program's rate tables and policy counts, and the agency's report to Congress.

briefs.headline: [UPDATE: airline_seat_rule] The airline seat size rule is finalized
briefs.brief:
What happened: The FAA finalized minimum seat dimensions for evacuation purposes, setting 28 inches of pitch and 17 inches of width.
Key facts: The standard matches what most carriers already fly. Two consumer groups called it too small and will comment in the reconsideration docket.
Context: Congress ordered the rule in 2018.
Sourcing: The final rule.

briefs.headline: [SIDE-COVERED: dam_safety] The Army Corps orders drawdowns at 41 dams it rates high hazard
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Army Corps of Engineers ordered reservoir levels lowered at 41 dams in twelve states after an inspection program found spillways or embankments unable to pass a design flood.
Key facts: About 2.4 million people live in the mapped inundation areas below the 41 dams. Drawdowns of 8 to 22 feet begin this month and cut hydropower output and municipal water storage for four cities, including one that draws 40 percent of its supply from an affected reservoir. Repairs are estimated at $7.8 billion against $900 million appropriated. The Corps says none of the dams is in danger of failing at current levels.
Context: The inspection program began in 2024 after a spillway failure in Missouri, and has covered 340 of the Corps' 700 dams.
Sourcing: The Corps' orders and inspection summaries, and the affected water utilities.

briefs.headline: Productivity: output per hour rose 2.3 percent in the third quarter
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Labor Department reported nonfarm productivity up 2.3 percent at an annual rate.
Key facts: Unit labor costs rose 1.1 percent. The department revised the second quarter up two tenths.
Context: Productivity growth has run above 2 percent for six quarters.
Sourcing: The department's release.

briefs.headline: Peru's congress removes the interior minister
briefs.brief:
What happened: Peru's congress voted to censure and remove the interior minister after a prison escape.
Key facts: The vote was 74 to 41. It is the fifth interior minister removed in two years.
Context: The president has named eleven cabinets since taking office.
Sourcing: The congressional record.
